title: Mount Sinai and the Ten Sayings
bigQuestion: What does the Torah say the people heard at the mountain, and how do Jewish families keep those words today?

story.title: One Rule for Our Room
story.kicker: A class writes its own rules, and then hears about a mountain where the Torah says ten sayings were given.
paragraphs: Ms. Ortiz's class sits on the rug. She holds up a big sheet of paper. It is blank. "Today we make rules for our room," she says. "Each of you will write one rule. It should make our room a better place."

Leo writes, "Take turns." Ana writes, "Tell the truth." Jamal writes, "Do not take what is not yours." Priya writes, "Be kind to helpers." Ms. Ortiz tapes each rule to the paper. Soon the paper is full.

"Rules are not just for our room," says Ms. Ortiz. "Long ago, the Torah says, a whole people stood at a mountain. They heard ten sayings. Some of them sound like yours." She reads one: "Honor your father and your mother."

Ana raises her hand. "Do people still keep those rules?" Ms. Ortiz nods. "Jewish families do. They even have a holiday to remember that day. It is called Shavuot." Leo looks at the class rules. "Ours should have a holiday too," he says.
story.think: Which rule would you write for your room? Why would it make the room a better place?

lessons.title: A Camp in the Wilderness
lessons.mainIdea: The Torah says the people walked to a mountain called Sinai and camped there.
reading: After the sea, the people kept walking. They were in the *wilderness*. That is a wild, dry place with no towns. The Torah says they walked for weeks.
Then they came to a mountain. Its name was Mount *Sinai*. The people set up their tents at the bottom. The whole people camped together.
The Torah says Moses went up the mountain. He came back with a message. The people said, "All that the LORD has spoken, we will do."

words.d: a wild, dry place with no towns; the people walked through it after Egypt
the mountain where the Torah says the people camped and heard the ten sayings

look.title: Counting the Journey
rows: Days of Passover in the Torah
look.cite: Exodus (Shemot) 7–12 and 12:15; Leviticus (Vayikra) 23:15–16, Jewish Publication Society translation, 1917

check.q: Where did the people camp, in the Torah's story?
choices: At the bottom of Mount Sinai
check.why: The Torah says the people set up their tents at the bottom of Mount Sinai.

check.q: Who does the Torah say went up the mountain?
check.why: The Torah says Moses went up Mount Sinai and came back with a message.

lessons.title: Thunder and a Cloud
lessons.mainIdea: The Torah says a thick cloud covered the mountain, and the people heard God speak.
reading: The Torah says the people got ready for three days. They washed their clothes. On the third day, there was *thunder*. There was lightning. A thick cloud sat on the mountain.
A loud horn sound grew louder and louder. The people shook. The Torah says God spoke from the mountain. Everyone heard.
Jewish tradition teaches that this is when the *Torah* was given. The story says God gave Moses the teaching to bring to the people.

words.d: the loud boom that comes with a storm; the Torah says thunder came at the mountain
the five books of teaching; Jewish tradition says it was given at Mount Sinai

look.title: Look at the Mountain
look.text: Look at the mountain. A thick gray cloud sits on top. You cannot see the top at all. Lightning flashes inside the cloud. A long horn sound rolls down the mountain. At the bottom, a crowd of people stands very still, holding hands.
look.prompt: How do you think the people at the bottom feel? What would you do if you were there?

check.q: What does the Torah say covered the mountain?
check.why: The Torah says a thick cloud sat on Mount Sinai, with thunder and lightning.

check.q: How many days did the people get ready?
check.why: The Torah says the people got ready for three days before the mountain shook.

check.q: What does Jewish tradition say was given at Mount Sinai?
check.why: Jewish tradition teaches that the Torah, the teaching, was given at Mount Sinai.

lessons.title: One God and a Day of Rest
lessons.mainIdea: The first sayings are about one God and about resting on Shabbat.
reading: Many people call them the Ten Commandments. Jewish tradition calls them the Ten *Sayings*. The first saying starts, "I am the LORD your God." It says God brought the people out of Egypt.
The next sayings say: there is one God. Do not make statues to bow to. Do not use God's name in a bad way.
Then comes *Shabbat*. Remember the seventh day. Rest on that day. Do not work. Jewish families keep this day every week with candles and bread.

words.d: what Jewish tradition calls the Ten Commandments; ten short words to live by
the seventh day, a day of rest; one of the ten sayings is to keep it

look.title: The Shabbat Saying
look.text: Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.
look.prompt: Sabbath is the English word for Shabbat. What does this saying ask people to do?

check.q: What does Jewish tradition call the Ten Commandments?
check.why: Jewish tradition calls them the Ten Sayings. The plagues were in Egypt.

check.q: How does the first saying begin?
choices: I am the LORD your God
check.why: The first saying starts, "I am the LORD your God," and tells of leaving Egypt.

check.q: What does the Shabbat saying ask people to do?
check.why: The saying says to remember the seventh day and rest. Jewish families call it Shabbat.

lessons.title: Family, Truth and What Is Yours
lessons.mainIdea: The other sayings are about how people treat each other.
reading: The first sayings are about God. The rest are about people. The fifth saying is to *honor* your father and your mother. To honor is to treat with care and respect.
Next: do not hurt or kill anyone. Be true to your family. Do not take what is not yours. Do not tell lies about your neighbor.
The last saying is, do not wish for what belongs to someone else. Jewish tradition teaches all ten sayings together. They are about God and about people.

words.d: to treat someone with care and respect; the fifth saying is to honor your parents

look.title: The Fifth Saying
look.text: Honour thy father and thy mother, that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.
look.prompt: "Thy" is an old word for "your." What is one way to honor a parent this week?

check.q: What does honor mean?
choices: To treat with care and respect
check.why: To honor is to treat with care and respect. The fifth saying is to honor your parents.

check.q: Which of these is one of the ten sayings?
choices: Do not take what is not yours
check.why: "Do not take what is not yours" is one of the sayings. The others are not.

check.q: What are the last sayings about?
check.why: The first sayings are about God. The rest are about how people treat each other.

lessons.title: What a Mitzvah Is
lessons.mainIdea: A mitzvah is a commandment in the Torah; Jewish tradition counts many of them.
reading: The ten sayings are not the only rules in the Torah. Each rule is called a *mitzvah*. That means a commandment. Something you are told to do, or not to do.
Some mitzvot are about God. Light candles for Shabbat. Some are about people. Help a person who is poor. Be kind to a stranger. Jewish tradition counts 613 mitzvot in the Torah.
Many Jewish people say "doing a mitzvah" when they do a good deed. Helping a friend carry books is a mitzvah. So is sharing.

words.d: a commandment in the Torah; many Jewish people also use it to mean a good deed

look.title: Counting the Rules
rows: Mitzvot in the Torah, as Jewish tradition counts them
look.cite: Exodus (Shemot) 20; the count of 613 is from the Talmud, Makkot 23b, as Jewish tradition teaches
look.prompt: Which number is the biggest? Is 613 more or less than 10?

check.q: What is a mitzvah?
check.why: A mitzvah is a commandment in the Torah. Many people also use it for a good deed.

check.q: How many mitzvot does Jewish tradition count in the Torah?
check.why: Jewish tradition counts 613 mitzvot in the Torah. Ten of them are the sayings.

check.q: Which of these could someone call a mitzvah?
check.why: Helping a friend is a good deed. Many Jewish people call a good deed a mitzvah.

lessons.title: Shavuot: Remembering the Mountain
lessons.mainIdea: Jewish families celebrate Shavuot to remember the day the Torah says the ten sayings were given.
reading: Seven weeks after Passover comes a holiday. It is called *Shavuot*. That means "weeks." Jewish tradition connects this day to Mount Sinai.
On Shavuot, many Jewish families go to the synagogue. They hear the ten sayings read aloud. Many stand up to listen.
Many families eat foods made with milk and cheese. Some decorate with flowers and green plants. Some stay up late to study the Torah. It is a happy day.

words.d: the holiday seven weeks after Passover; Jewish tradition links it to the giving of the Torah

look.title: Two Holidays, One Story
look.text: Look at two tables. The first is a Passover table. There is matzah and a Haggadah. The story is about leaving Egypt. The second is a Shavuot table, seven weeks later. There are flowers and a cheese blintz. The story is about a mountain and ten sayings.
look.prompt: Which table comes first in the year? Which part of the story comes first?

check.q: What does Shavuot mean?
check.why: Shavuot means "weeks." It comes seven weeks after Passover.

check.q: What does Jewish tradition connect Shavuot to?
check.why: Jewish tradition connects Shavuot to the day the Torah was given at Mount Sinai.

check.q: What do many families eat on Shavuot?
check.why: Many Jewish families eat foods made with milk and cheese on Shavuot.

lessons.title: The Torah Scroll in the Synagogue
lessons.mainIdea: In a synagogue, the Torah is a big scroll kept in a special cabinet and read aloud.
reading: A *synagogue* is where Jewish people meet to pray and learn. At the front is a special cabinet. It is called the ark. Inside the ark is the Torah *scroll*.
The scroll is rolled on two wooden poles. It has a cover like a coat. When it is carried, people stand up. A reader uses a little pointer to keep the place.
The words are written in Hebrew by hand. The reader chants them out loud. Each week a new part is read. The whole scroll takes one year.

words.d: the place where Jewish people meet to pray and learn
a long roll of paper or skin; the Torah is written on one

look.title: Look at the Scroll
look.text: Look at the front of the room. The doors of the ark open. Inside stands a tall scroll in a velvet cover. A silver crown sits on top. A person lifts it out. Everyone in the room stands up. The cover comes off. The scroll is rolled open on a table.
look.prompt: Why do you think people stand up when the scroll is carried?

check.q: What is a synagogue?
choices: Where Jewish people meet to pray and learn
check.why: A synagogue is the place where Jewish people meet to pray and learn.

check.q: Where is the Torah scroll kept in the synagogue?
check.why: The Torah scroll is kept in a special cabinet called the ark.

check.q: What do people do when the scroll is carried?
check.why: When the Torah scroll is carried, people in the synagogue stand up.
